L22: ### y sus beneficios en la salud

L29: #### Estudios científicos avanzados:
L30: 
L31: Nuestra investigacion se centra en entender cómo los ingredientes bioactivos de los hongos pueden mejorar la salud animal.

L34: #### Ensayos clínicos rigurosos:
L35: 
L36: Hemos realizados ensayos clínicos con profesionales veterinarios que avalan su excelente tolerancia en tratamientos crónicos.
L37:

L39: #### Innovación constante:
L40: 
L41: Desarrollamos nuevas fórmulas y tratamientos que realmente funcionan, basándonos en los últimos avances científicos.

L43: Nuestros productos están basados en la

L58: ## Hifas Onco Pet
L59: 
L60: Estudio clínico: Uso de Hifas Onco Pet en gatos con Carcinoma de Células Escamosas (CCE)
L61: 
L62: En el ensayo clínico realizado por Sara Peña Acreditada AVEPA en Dermatología SkinVet, conocimos a Tato, un felino rescatado de la calle, de unos 13 años de edad. Presentaba una lesión en el plano nasal y el belfo y en la analítica de sangre se le detectó leucocitosis, monocitosis, linfocitosis e hiperglobulinemia. Se relacionaron estos resultados con la lesión inflamatoria nasal.
L63: Tras someterse a un tratamiento de electroquimioterapia bajo anestesia general, Tato recibió nuestro jarabe en nanoemulsión HIFAS ONCO PET® como parte de su recuperación postoperatoria. A los 90 días del estudio, la lesión mostraba una recuperación completa, sin signos de recidiva ni nuevas lesiones. Además, Tato aumentó de peso y mantuvo un excelente apetito durante todo el proceso.

L46: # Ongoing EU Clinical Trials
L47: ESVONC attaches great importance to innovation and evidence-based medicine in the field of veterinary oncology. Therefore, we are happy to share with you with a monthly overview of ongoing canine and feline oncology trials in Europe. We are convinced that knowledge of these trials will enhance collaboration between researchers and clinicians, thus increasing recruitment for clinical trials and treatment options for dogs and cats.
L48: Please find below a non-exhaustive listing of ongoing trials as gathered in the Oncowaf database. For more details about these trials, please visit 【45†https://oncowaf.be/en/ClinicalTrials†oncowaf.be】.
L49: If you have an ongoing clinical trial and would like to add it to the Oncowaf clinical trial database and this mailing, please contact contact@oncowaf.com. This list is an intiative of dr. Laetitia Cicchelero (DVM, PhD, Cross-health coordinator @ Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, Ghent University). Laetitia is initiator and inspirer of ONCOWAF. ESVONC wishes to thank Laetitia for her efforts to create this useful overview.
L50: This list is updated on a monthly basis.

L27: How can I find an ongoing clinical trial?
L28: 
L29: Via the search button, you can perform a targeted search for canine clinical trials. In order to do this, tick -if known- the box of your dog’s tumour type (‘Select tumour type’) and/or the countries (‘Select location’) for which you wish to know whether clinical trials are ongoing.

L31: Afterwards, a list of trials for which your dog might be eligible will appear. The listed information is limited to
L32:   * Treatment centre where the trial is available
L33:   * In/exclusion criteria. Inclusion criteria describe the criteria necessary for your dog to participate in the trial (e.g. inoperable tumour). Exclusion criteria describe conditions that exclude possible participation to the trial (e.g. concomitant chemotherapy).
L34:   * Contact information: phone number and e-mail address of the trial’s contact person, webpage with more information on the trial.
L35: For more details on the trial, we recommend you to contact the researchers via the listed contact info.

L19: # Clinical Trials for Dogs with Cancer
L20: 
L21: Links last verified: August 20, 2026
L22: ## Explore Current Research Trials in Canine Oncology
L23: 
L24: When a beloved dog is diagnosed with cancer, many families ask whether a clinical trial may provide an additional option. Canine oncology studies are conducted throughout the United States and around the world, but identifying an appropriate trial, and participating in one, can sometimes be challenging.
L25: 
L26: Each clinical trial has specific eligibility requirements.
L27: 
L28: These may include:
L29:   * A dog’s breed
L30:   * Age
L31:   * Weight
L32:   * Overall health
L33:   * Life expectancy
L34:   * Cancer type
L35:   * Cancer stage
L36:   * Previous care
L37:   * ...and other medical factors
L38: 
L39: Meeting a study’s general description does not guarantee acceptance. Pet parents should speak directly with the research team and their veterinary care provider to determine whether a trial may be appropriate for their dog.
L40: 
L41: It is also important to understand that clinical trials are not always free.

L27: # Canine Clinical Trials
L28: 
L29: 【5†Why enroll your dog in a clinical trial?】【6†About Canine Oncology Clinical Trials】【7†Find a Canine Clinical Trial】
L30: ## Why enroll your dog in a clinical trial?
L31: 
L32: Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone tumor of dogs. Nearly 10,000 dogs are diagnosed with this cancer each year.  The incidence of 【8†osteosarcoma in dogs†www.csuanimalcancercenter.org】 is anywhere from 10-50x higher than in humans.  Research in dogs will one day mean better treatment for kids.
L33: Enrolling a dog in a clinical trial can offer several potential benefits to both the individual pet and the broader veterinary community. Here are some reasons why pet owners may consider enrolling their dogs in clinical trials:
L34:   * Access to Cutting-Edge Treatments: Clinical trials often investigate novel treatments, therapies, or medications that are not yet available to the general public. By participating in a clinical trial, pet owners may gain access to potentially more effective or advanced treatments for their dog's condition.
L35:   * Contributing to Scientific Knowledge: Clinical trials are essential for advancing veterinary medicine. By participating, pet owners help researchers gather data and evidence that can lead to new understandings of diseases, improved treatments, and better overall care for animals in the future.
L36:   * Expert Monitoring and Care: Dogs enrolled in clinical trials receive close monitoring and care from experienced veterinarians and researchers. This regular attention can be beneficial in managing the dog's health and detecting any changes or side effects early on.
L37:   * Potential Cost Savings: In some cases, the cost of participating in a clinical trial may be partially or fully covered by the sponsoring organization. This can ease the financial burden on pet owners, especially when dealing with expensive medical treatments.
L38: 
L39:   * Supportive Community: Pet owners in clinical trials become part of a supportive community of other caregivers and veterinary professionals who are invested in finding solutions and improving the health outcomes for animals.

L67: What is a Clinical Trial?
L68: A clinical trial is a research study in which animals with cancer participate to evaluate aspects of, or novel treatments for, cancer. Well-designed clinical trials can answer questions about preventing, detecting, and treating cancer that help many animals in the future. Trials are designed to minimize risk to the participants, but drug trials often involve new anti-cancer agents that may not have been used in companion animals, and the extent of possible toxicity is not known.
L69: There are four phases of clinical trials to safely and methodically evaluate promising new treatments.
L70: Phase 1 trials are typically conducted in a small group of animals (6-12) with cancer to test a new treatment that has never been tried in a clinical patient. The goals are to evaluate safety and side effects, and to determine the dose and way to use the treatment. It is important to remember that no therapeutic benefit is expected in a phase 1 trial.
L71: Phase 2 trials use information from phase 1 trials to use the new treatment at a given dose and schedule in a larger group of animals with cancer (usually 20-40). The goal of a phase 2 trial is to determine efficacy of the new treatment and further evaluate safety. In cancer clinical trials, a phase 2 trial is intended to determine what types of cancer will respond or how well a given cancer responds to a new therapy.
L72: Phase 3 trials compare the new treatment to standard treatment options in a large group of animals with cancer. The goal is to determine whether the new treatment is better than other common treatments and to further monitor safety and side effects.
L73: 
L74: Phase 4 trials compare two or more well-established treatment regimes in a given group of patients, typically after the treatment has already been approved for use (in people) or in common use (in animals).
